title: Passé composé with avoir
description: Say what you did, didn’t do and have already done with avoir.

guide.summary: The passé composé says what you did and finished. Most verbs build it with the present of avoir plus a past participle, so you need two things: avoir’s forms and the participle of your verb.

sections.title: The two parts: avoir + participle
sections.text: The passé composé is always two words: the present of avoir, then the past participle. The participle never changes for the subject.
steps: Find the subject and take its form of avoir.
Add the past participle of the verb, never the infinitive.
Write je as j’ before ai.
watch: The participle does not agree with the subject: nous avons mangé, never mangés.
With -er verbs the participle and the infinitive sound the same: parlé, parler.
Être itself is conjugated with avoir: j’ai été.

sections.title: Regular participles: which ending?
sections.text: Regular verbs make their participle from the infinitive ending. Three endings cover all of them.
steps: Look at the last two letters of the infinitive.
Take that row and swap the infinitive ending for the participle ending.
Put the subject's form of avoir in front.
watch: Do not mix the endings: fine, finé, attendi and attendé do not exist.
After the auxiliary write the participle, not the infinitive: j’ai travaillé, not j’ai travailler.

sections.title: Irregular participles ending in a consonant
sections.text: Many everyday verbs have a short participle ending in a silent consonant. Learn these one by one.
steps: Check whether the verb is on this list before applying a regular ending.
Take the participle as it stands; the final consonant is silent.
Put the subject's form of avoir in front.
watch: Ouvrir and offrir look like -ir verbs but do not take -i.
Prendre looks like an -re verb but does not take -u.
Do not use the present tense form: il met, il prend, elle dit are not participles.

sections.title: Short irregular participles (mostly -u)
sections.text: These come mainly from -oir and -re verbs. Être is the odd one out, and it still takes avoir as its auxiliary.
steps: Look the verb up here instead of guessing a regular ending.
Keep the written accent or cedilla the participle carries.
Remember that avoir and être are both conjugated with avoir.
watch: Do not build these from the present stem: buvu, lisé and recevu are not words.
Dû keeps its circumflex and reçu keeps its cedilla.
Avoir is its own auxiliary: j’ai eu.

sections.title: Saying you didn’t do it
sections.text: Ne…pas wraps the auxiliary only. The participle stays outside, right after pas.
steps: Build the positive sentence first.
Put ne in front of the auxiliary and pas immediately after it.
Elide ne to n’ before ai, as, a, avons, avez and ont.

examples.fr: Elle n’a pas pris le bus.

watch: Pas never goes after the participle.
Dropping ne (j’ai pas vu) is casual speech; in writing keep both halves.

sections.title: Where short adverbs go
sections.text: Short common adverbs sit between the auxiliary and the participle, where English puts them after the verb.
steps: Build the passé composé: auxiliary, then participle.
Slide the short adverb in between the two.
In a negative sentence, keep it after pas and before the participle.
watch: Time expressions stay outside the verb: j’ai travaillé hier soir.
Moving the adverb to the front of the sentence does not fix its place.

sections.title: Asking with inversion
sections.text: Only the auxiliary swaps with the subject pronoun, joined by a hyphen. The participle and the rest of the sentence stay put.
steps: Find the auxiliary in the statement.
Move it in front of the subject pronoun and join them with a hyphen.
Add -t- when a meets il, elle or on.
Leave the participle and the rest of the sentence after the subject.

examples.en: Have you already read this book?

watch: Est-ce que and a simple rising tone also make questions: est-ce que tu as vu Paul ?
The linking letter is -t-, with a hyphen on each side, never an apostrophe.

sections.title: When the participle agrees
sections.text: With avoir the participle ignores the subject. It agrees only with a direct object placed before the verb: le, la, l’, les or que.

rows: les livres : je les ai lus
les photos : je les ai vues

steps: Find the direct object of the verb.
Ask whether it stands before the auxiliary (a pronoun le, la, l’, les, or que).
If it does, match the participle to its gender and number; if it comes after, change nothing.

examples.fr: Ces photos ? Je les ai vues hier.
examples.en: These photos? I saw them yesterday.

watch: The subject never triggers agreement with avoir: elles ont mangé.
You hear the agreement only after a consonant (prise, écrite, ouverte); in vues it is silent but still written.

Add the subject's form of avoir, even for avoir and être themselves.

Put ne before it and pas straight after it.
Elide ne before a vowel, and leave the participle after pas.
Split the verb into its two parts: auxiliary and participle.
Place the short adverb between them, not after the participle.
In a negative sentence, keep it after pas.
Find the auxiliary in the statement.
Put it in front of the subject pronoun with a hyphen.
Insert -t- if the auxiliary ends in a vowel and the subject is il, elle or on.
Keep the participle and the rest of the sentence after the subject.
Find the direct object and check whether it comes before the verb.
If it does, work out its gender and number.
Add the matching ending to the participle; add nothing when the object follows the verb.

exercises.hint: Use the present of avoir for nous, then the -er participle.
exercises.feedback: Two words: the auxiliary avoir for nous and a participle ending in -é.
exercises.explanation: Nous takes avons, and manger becomes mangé: nous avons mangé.

mistakes.why: Manger is the infinitive. After the auxiliary French needs the past participle, which sounds the same but is spelt differently.
Ai is the je form of avoir. The subject asked for here is nous, which has its own form of the auxiliary.
This adds a plural -s for nous, but with avoir the participle never agrees with the subject.
Sommes is être. Manger builds its past with avoir, like most verbs.

exercises.instruction: Write regarder in the passé composé (auxiliary and participle).
exercises.hint: Tu goes with the tu form of avoir. An -er verb’s participle ends in -é.
exercises.feedback: Write both parts: avoir for tu, then the participle.
exercises.explanation: Tu as regardé: as is avoir for tu, and regarder becomes regardé.

mistakes.why: Regarder is the infinitive. The passé composé needs the past participle after the auxiliary, spelt differently even though it sounds the same.
A is the il/elle form of avoir, for one other person. The subject here is tu.
Es is être. Regarder forms its past with avoir.
That is only half of the verb. The passé composé is two words, and the auxiliary comes first.

exercises.source: Elle a ____ sa mère au téléphone.
exercises.hint: After the auxiliary a you need the past participle.
exercises.feedback: The infinitive and the present tense cannot follow the auxiliary.
exercises.explanation: The passé composé is auxiliary + participle, so a appelé. The -er participle ends in -é.

mistakes.why: That is the infinitive, the dictionary form. After the auxiliary a, French needs a past participle.
Appelle is the present tense: elle appelle means she is calling. The auxiliary a is already there, so what follows must be a participle.

exercises.instruction: Build the sentence: We bought some bread.
exercises.hint: Start with the subject and the auxiliary, then the participle.
exercises.feedback: The verb after avons must be a participle, not an infinitive.
exercises.explanation: Nous avons acheté: avoir for nous plus the participle acheté.

mistakes.why: Acheter is the infinitive. After avons the verb must take its past participle form.
The auxiliary is missing. Without avoir this is not a passé composé at all.

exercises.hint: Look at the word after the auxiliary.
exercises.feedback: After ai you need a past participle, not the infinitive. They sound the same but are spelt differently.
exercises.explanation: The passé composé uses the participle travaillé, not the infinitive travailler.

mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged: the infinitive is still sitting after the auxiliary.
Travaille without an accent is the present tense (je travaille). Here the verb is finished and past.
Je never stays whole in front of a vowel; it is shortened with an apostrophe.

exercises.hint: Finir is a regular -ir verb. Think of the ending of its participle.
exercises.feedback: Use avoir for vous and a participle ending in -i.
exercises.explanation: Vous takes avez, and regular -ir verbs like finir make their participle in -i: fini.

mistakes.why: The -é ending belongs to -er verbs like parler. Finir is a regular -ir verb.
The -u ending belongs to regular -re verbs like vendre. Finir does not end in -re.
As is the tu form of avoir. The subject asked for here is vous.
Êtes is être. Finir builds its passé composé with avoir.

exercises.hint: Attendre is a regular -re verb. Its participle ends in -u.
exercises.feedback: Use avoir for ils, then the -re participle.
exercises.explanation: Ils takes ont, and attendre becomes attendu: ils ont attendu.

mistakes.why: The -i ending belongs to regular -ir verbs like finir. Attendre ends in -re.
The -é ending only happens with -er verbs, and attendre is not one.
That is the infinitive. After the auxiliary the verb must take its participle form.
A is the il/elle form of avoir, for one person. Ils is plural.
Sont is être; attendre takes avoir. Sont attendu would also mean they are being awaited.

exercises.hint: Finir is a regular -ir verb.
exercises.feedback: Regular -ir verbs do not end their participle in -é or -u.
exercises.explanation: Regular -ir verbs drop -r: finir becomes fini.

mistakes.why: The -é ending is for -er participles like parlé. Finir is an -ir verb.
The -u ending is for regular -re participles like vendu. Finir does not end in -re.

exercises.source: Il a ____ un bruit dans la cuisine.
exercises.hint: Entendre is a regular -re verb.
exercises.feedback: Regular -re verbs form the participle with -u.
exercises.explanation: Regular -re verbs replace -re with -u: entendre becomes entendu.

mistakes.why: The -i ending belongs to regular -ir verbs like finir. Entendre ends in -re.
The -é ending belongs to -er verbs. Entendre is not one of them.

exercises.source: Vous avez répondi à la lettre.
answers: Vous avez répondu à la lettre.
exercises.hint: Répondre is a regular -re verb.
exercises.feedback: Check the ending of the participle.
exercises.explanation: Répondre ends in -re, so its participle ends in -u: répondu.

answers: Vous avez répondi à la lettre.
mistakes.why: Nothing has changed. That is still the -ir ending, but répondre is a regular -re verb.

answers: Vous avez répondé à la lettre.
mistakes.why: The -é ending belongs to -er verbs, and répondre does not belong to that group.

answers: Vous avez répondre à la lettre.
mistakes.why: That leaves the infinitive after the auxiliary; the past needs a participle.

answers: Vous êtes répondu à la lettre.
mistakes.why: Être is the wrong auxiliary here: répondre forms its past with avoir.

mistakes.why: The -i ending is for regular -ir verbs like finir. Perdre ends in -re.
The -é ending is for -er verbs only, and perdre is not one.
Je must elide before a vowel: it loses its e and takes an apostrophe.
That is the infinitive after the auxiliary. The passé composé needs the participle.

exercises.hint: Faire has an irregular participle. Je elides before a vowel.
exercises.feedback: The participle of faire does not end in -é.
exercises.explanation: Faire has the irregular participle fait: j’ai fait.

That is the infinitive. After the auxiliary the verb must take its participle form.
As is the tu form of avoir. The subject asked for here is je.
Je never stays whole before a vowel; it is shortened with an apostrophe.

exercises.instruction: Write mettre in the passé composé (auxiliary and participle).
exercises.hint: Mettre has a short irregular participle, like prendre.
exercises.feedback: Write avoir for il, then the irregular participle of mettre.
exercises.explanation: Il takes a, and mettre has the irregular participle mis: il a mis.

mistakes.why: That applies the regular -re rule, but mettre is irregular and its participle is much shorter.
Met is the present tense (il met son manteau). The participle of mettre ends in a different consonant.
That is the infinitive after the auxiliary; the passé composé needs a participle.
Est is être. Mettre builds its past with avoir.
Ont is the ils/elles form of avoir. The subject il is one person.

exercises.hint: Ouvrir has an irregular participle ending in a consonant.
exercises.feedback: Ouvrir does not follow the regular -ir pattern.
exercises.explanation: Ouvrir has the irregular participle ouvert: j’ai ouvert.

mistakes.why: That is the regular -ir ending, but ouvrir is irregular: its participle ends in a consonant.
The -é ending belongs to -er verbs. Ouvrir is an -ir verb, and an irregular one.

exercises.hint: Offrir works like ouvrir.
exercises.feedback: Offrir does not follow the regular -ir pattern.
exercises.explanation: Offrir, like ouvrir, has an irregular participle ending in -ert: offert.

mistakes.why: That is the regular -ir ending. Offrir behaves like ouvrir, whose participle is irregular.
The -é ending belongs to -er verbs, and offrir is not one.

exercises.instruction: Translate into French, using the passé composé.
exercises.hint: Dire has a short irregular participle.
exercises.feedback: Use avoir for elle and the participle of dire.
exercises.explanation: Dire has the irregular participle dit: elle a dit oui.

mistakes.why: That is the present tense: she says yes. A finished past action needs the auxiliary plus a participle.
That leaves the infinitive after the auxiliary; the passé composé needs a participle.
Dis is the je/tu present form (je dis, tu dis), not a participle.
Est is être. Dire forms its past with avoir.

exercises.hint: Prendre is irregular. Its participle does not end in -u.
exercises.feedback: Prendre does not follow the -re → -u pattern.
exercises.explanation: Prendre and its family (apprendre, comprendre) have the participle pris: j’ai pris.

mistakes.why: Nothing has changed. That applies the regular -re rule, and prendre does not follow it.
That is the infinitive after the auxiliary; the past needs a participle.
Prend is the present tense (il prend le bus), not a participle.
The -é ending belongs to -er verbs. Prendre is neither an -er verb nor a regular one.

exercises.hint: Boire has a very short participle ending in -u.
exercises.feedback: Use avoir for tu and the irregular participle of boire.
exercises.explanation: Boire has the participle bu: tu as bu.

mistakes.why: Bois is the present tense (tu bois). The participle of boire is a single short syllable.
That is the infinitive. After the auxiliary the verb takes its participle form.
Boire does not build its participle from the stem buv-; the real one is much shorter.
A is the il/elle form of avoir. The subject asked for here is tu.
Es is être. Boire forms its past with avoir.

exercises.hint: Être itself takes avoir in the passé composé.
exercises.feedback: Être is conjugated with avoir, and its participle is irregular.
exercises.explanation: Être uses avoir as its auxiliary, and its participle is été: vous avez été.

mistakes.why: Être is not its own auxiliary: like most verbs it builds its past with avoir.
Était is the imparfait (il était). What follows the auxiliary must be a participle.
As is the tu form of avoir. The subject asked for here is vous.
That is the infinitive. After the auxiliary the verb needs its participle form.

exercises.instruction: Write recevoir in the passé composé (auxiliary and participle).
exercises.hint: Recevoir has a participle ending in -u, with a cedilla before u.
exercises.feedback: Write avoir for elle and the irregular participle of recevoir.
exercises.explanation: Recevoir has the participle reçu; the cedilla keeps the soft s sound before u.

mistakes.why: Recevoir does not keep its recev- stem in the participle; the real one is shorter.
That is the infinitive after the auxiliary. The past needs a participle.
Reçoit is the present tense (elle reçoit une lettre), not a participle.
Est is être, and this also turns the sentence into a passive: recevoir forms its past with avoir.
Ont is the ils/elles form of avoir. Elle is one person.

exercises.hint: Lire has a very short participle.
exercises.feedback: Lire does not form its participle from lis- or with -i.
exercises.explanation: Lire has the irregular participle lu: tu as lu.

mistakes.why: That builds a participle from the present stem lis- with an -er ending. Lire does neither.
The -i ending belongs to regular -ir verbs like finir, and lire is not one.

exercises.instruction: Translate into French, using the passé composé.
exercises.hint: Avoir is its own auxiliary. Its participle is only two letters.
exercises.feedback: You need avoir twice: as the auxiliary and as the participle.
exercises.explanation: Avoir has the participle eu, so nous avons eu (or on a eu) un problème.

mistakes.why: That is the present tense: we have a problem. A finished past needs the auxiliary plus a participle.
Avoir does not make its participle by adding -u to the infinitive; its real participle is only two letters.
That leaves the infinitive after the auxiliary; the passé composé needs a participle.
Sommes is être. Avoir is its own auxiliary, so it uses avoir here too.
Été is the participle of être, so this says we were a problem. The English verb is have.

exercises.instruction: Build the sentence: He had to work.
exercises.hint: Devoir has a short participle ending in -u, with an accent.
exercises.feedback: Choose the real participle of devoir, then the infinitive.
exercises.explanation: Devoir has the participle dû (with a circumflex), followed by an infinitive: il a dû travailler.

mistakes.why: Devu applies the regular -re rule to devoir, which is irregular; its real participle carries a written accent.
This drops the verb devoir altogether. Had to work needs a participle before the infinitive.

answers: Je n’ai pas vu le film.

exercises.hint: Ne and pas go around the auxiliary, not the participle.

exercises.explanation: In the passé composé, ne…pas surrounds the auxiliary: je n’ai pas vu.

exercises.instruction: Complete the negative sentence. Write the missing part before pas.

exercises.feedback: Ne comes right before the auxiliary and elides before a vowel.

Ont is the ils/elles form of avoir. Elle is one person.
That is only the auxiliary. The first half of the negation is missing in front of it.

exercises.feedback: The participle stays outside ne…pas.

exercises.feedback: Look for the form with -t- between the auxiliary and the pronoun.
exercises.explanation: A-t-elle: the -t- separates the two vowels.

mistakes.why: Two vowels meet across the hyphen, which French avoids here; a linking consonant is needed.
That keeps the subject first and only adds a hyphen. Inversion puts the auxiliary in front of the pronoun.

exercises.instruction: Translate into French, using the passé composé.
exercises.source: Did you (to a friend) see Paul?
answers: Est-ce que tu as vu Paul ?

alternatives.message: T’as is casual spoken French. In writing, use tu as: Tu as vu Paul ? (or As-tu vu Paul ?).

exercises.hint: Did you see is a passé composé question with tu.
exercises.feedback: Use tu with avoir and the participle of voir.
exercises.explanation: Voir has the participle vu. Inversion (as-tu vu), est-ce que or rising intonation all make the question.

mistakes.why: Voir is the infinitive. The question still needs a participle after the subject.
That is the formal you. The task says to a friend, so the informal subject is needed.
Inversion needs a hyphen between the auxiliary and the pronoun.
Es is être. Voir forms its past with avoir.

exercises.instruction: Build the question: Did you (formal) sleep well?
exercises.hint: Start with the inverted auxiliary and subject.
exercises.feedback: The adverb still goes before the participle.
exercises.explanation: Avez-vous inverts the auxiliary and subject; bien stays between it and dormi.

mistakes.why: The adverb has been fronted. In this question it stays inside the verb, before the participle.
The adverb has been left after the participle, as in English. It belongs between the two verb parts.
The adverb has been left out, so the question no longer asks how you slept.

exercises.instruction: Fix the error in the inversion.
exercises.hint: Two vowels meet across the hyphen.
exercises.feedback: French adds a linking letter between a and il.
exercises.explanation: A-t-il répondu ?: -t- is inserted when the verb ends in a vowel before il, elle or on.

mistakes.why: Nothing has changed: two vowels still meet across the hyphen and need a linking consonant.
The linking letter is attached with a hyphen on each side, not with an apostrophe.
That turns it back into a statement with a question mark. The task is to repair the inversion, not remove it.

exercises.source: Ces photos ? Je les ai ____ hier.
exercises.hint: Les comes before the verb. What does les stand for?
exercises.feedback: A direct object before avoir makes the participle agree with it.
exercises.explanation: Les stands for ces photos (feminine plural) and comes before the verb, so vu agrees: vues.

mistakes.why: That is the bare participle with no agreement. Les stands for ces photos and comes before the verb, so the participle must match it.
That marks the plural but leaves the word masculine. Photos is a feminine noun.

exercises.source: La lettre que j’ai ____ est sur la table.
exercises.hint: Que refers back to la lettre, which comes before the verb.
exercises.feedback: When que (a direct object) comes first, the participle agrees with what it refers to.
exercises.explanation: Que stands for la lettre (feminine singular), placed before the verb, so écrit becomes écrite.

mistakes.why: That is the bare participle. Que stands for la lettre, placed before the verb, so an ending is needed.
That is masculine plural. Lettre is one thing, and it is feminine.

exercises.hint: Where is the direct object: before or after the verb?
exercises.feedback: Agreement happens only when the direct object comes before the verb.
exercises.explanation: La voiture comes after the verb, so the participle does not agree: elle a lavé la voiture. The subject never matters with avoir.

mistakes.why: This adds a feminine ending, but agreement only happens when the direct object comes before the verb. La voiture comes after it.
This adds a masculine plural ending. Nothing here is plural, and the object follows the verb anyway.

exercises.instruction: Write the past participle of voir, with any agreement.
exercises.source: Ta sœur ? Je l’ai ____ (voir) au marché.
exercises.hint: L’ stands for ta sœur and comes before the verb.
exercises.feedback: The participle agrees with a direct object pronoun placed before it.
exercises.explanation: L’ means ta sœur (feminine singular), so vu takes -e: je l’ai vue.

mistakes.why: That is the bare participle. L’ stands for ta sœur and sits before the verb, so the participle must show her gender.
That is feminine plural. Ta sœur is one person.
That is masculine plural, and neither the gender nor the number fits ta sœur.
That is the infinitive. The blank needs the past participle.
Vois is the present tense (je vois). After the auxiliary you need a participle.

exercises.instruction: Replace la clé with a pronoun.
exercises.hint: The pronoun goes before the auxiliary. Then check the participle.
exercises.feedback: Once the object moves in front of the verb, the participle agrees with it.
exercises.explanation: La clé becomes l’ before ai, and pris agrees with the feminine object: je l’ai prise.

mistakes.why: The pronoun has moved but the participle has not changed. A direct object in front of avoir makes it agree.
Nothing has been replaced: the noun is still spelt out after the verb.
La must elide before a vowel: it loses its a and takes an apostrophe.
That is a plural ending, but only one key is being replaced.

exercises.source: Les fleurs que tu as acheté sont belles.
answers: Les fleurs que tu as achetées sont belles.
exercises.hint: What does que refer to, and where is it?
exercises.feedback: The participle must agree with the direct object placed before it.
exercises.explanation: Que stands for les fleurs (feminine plural), before the verb, so acheté becomes achetées.

answers: Les fleurs que tu as acheté sont belles.
mistakes.why: Nothing has changed. Que stands for les fleurs and comes before the verb, so the participle still has to agree.

answers: Les fleurs que tu as achetés sont belles.
mistakes.why: That marks the plural but leaves the word masculine, and fleurs is feminine.

answers: Les fleurs que tu as achetée sont belles.
mistakes.why: That marks the feminine but keeps it singular, and les fleurs is more than one.

answers: Les fleurs que tu as acheter sont belles.
mistakes.why: That is the infinitive. After the auxiliary the passé composé needs a participle.
